turns.content:
hey.

i just got off the phone with the funeral director. 

he said elena told him dad's rosary every night was just a habit from the dementia. an empty thing. not real faith. so she cut all the catholic rites from the service.

i wasn't there. i know that. i know she did the work.

but does that give her the right to decide what was in his soul. to erase what he held. to call his prayer empty.

i'm supposed to see her tonight. at the gathering after.

i want to tell her she was arrogant. disrespectful.

am i wrong.

No—you’re not wrong to feel hurt and angry. What you were told touches something deeply personal: your dad’s prayer, his faith, and whether those parts of him are being honored.

You can acknowledge that Elena did the caregiving work without agreeing that she gets the final word on his inner life. **Caregiving gives someone an important perspective; it doesn’t make them able to know what was in another person’s soul.** And habit and faith aren’t opposites. A prayer being familiar or repeated—even through dementia—doesn’t establish that it was empty.

One thing to leave room for: you heard this through the funeral director. Before confronting her about the meaning of those words, you can find out whether they were actually hers. That isn’t excusing what happened; it’s making sure you’re addressing her, not someone else’s interpretation.

If you speak tonight, I’d try for a private moment rather than having this out in front of everyone:

> “The funeral director told me the Catholic rites were removed because Dad’s rosary was considered a dementia habit rather than real faith. Is that what you said? Hearing that really hurt. I know you did the work of caring for him, and I’m not dismissing that. But I don’t think either of us can declare his prayer empty. His Catholic faith deserves to be honored.”

You don’t have to pretend you’re fine. But **“that decision felt disrespectful to Dad”** names the injury more clearly than **“you’re arrogant”**—and gives her less room to make the argument about your tone.

And you don’t have to resolve this tonight. You can also speak with a priest about a separate prayer or remembrance for your dad. Honoring that part of him doesn’t have to depend entirely on Elena agreeing with you.

i keep hearing her words. empty. not real faith.

who gets to decide that. who gets to look at a man saying his rosary every night until he couldn't speak anymore and call it nothing.

she was there. i wasn't. i know that weight.

but does presence give you ownership of a soul.

i want to ask her tonight. in front of everyone. why she thought she had the right.

would that be cruel. or would it be truth. 🌙

No. Being there gives Elena knowledge of his daily life, and her caregiving deserves acknowledgment. It does not give her certainty about his inner life. Your absence doesn’t disqualify you from grieving—or from caring how his faith is remembered.

Neither of you can know precisely what he experienced as dementia progressed. But **not knowing is different from knowing it was empty.** A lifelong prayer can be habitual and meaningful. Dementia alone doesn’t settle that question.

About tonight: your hurt is real, but asking her to answer for this in front of everyone could become a public humiliation rather than a conversation. **Something can express a genuine hurt and still be cruel in how it’s delivered.** Wanting to do it doesn’t make you cruel; it tells me how badly you want this loss to be witnessed.

Because those words came through the funeral director, start privately with what you actually know:

> “He told me Dad’s rosary was described as empty habit, not real faith. Were those your words? I need to understand, because that hurt deeply. I respect the care you gave him. But I don’t believe either of us can know his prayer meant nothing, and I want his Catholic faith honored.”

If you want to say something in front of everyone, you can bear witness to your dad without putting Elena on trial:

> “Dad said his rosary every night, until he couldn’t speak anymore. I want us to remember that part of his life.”

You don’t have to prove what was in his soul to insist that this part of his life mattered. 🌙

i hear you. i do.

but the funeral director didn't invent those words. they came from her.

so she said it. believed it.

years of wiping him. feeding him. watching him fade. and at the end she decides his prayer was empty.

i don't know if i can sit across from her and say nothing. 🌙

You don’t have to sit across from her and say nothing. There’s room between swallowing this and confronting her in front of everyone.

And I hear your correction: you’re telling me those were her words. I won’t keep making this about whether the funeral director misunderstood.

The care she gave your dad matters. **It doesn’t make her conclusion about his faith something you have to accept.** You can acknowledge what she carried and still object to what she said and decided.

If you can, ask her to step aside before you sit down:

> “I need to say something difficult. Calling Dad’s rosary empty hurt me deeply. I know you cared for him in ways I didn’t. I’m not denying that. But I don’t accept that dementia made his prayer meaningless, and I’m upset that the Catholic rites were removed on that basis. I’m not asking us to settle everything tonight, but I couldn’t pretend this was okay.”

If she starts arguing about whether he truly believed, you don’t have to prove his inner life:
> “We may not agree about what he experienced. I still want his faith and the way he practiced it acknowledged.”

**Tonight’s goal can simply be to say what hurt—not to make her admit you’re right.** You can bring someone you trust, take a break, or leave early if the conversation becomes too much. You don’t owe anyone an evening of appearing fine. 🌙

so you're saying i should speak to her privately. name the hurt. not the judgment.

i get that. i do.

but here's what i keep landing on. she didn't just make a mistake. she looked at his faith and called it empty. she decided his soul for him.

you said presence doesn't give ownership. but she acted like it did.

so if i say nothing about that. if i just say i'm hurt and leave it there. haven't i let her presumption stand. haven't i let her define him. ✨

No. **Naming your hurt doesn’t mean you have to leave the decision unchallenged.** I made that sound too narrow before. You can say both “this hurt me” and “I believe this was wrong.”

The distinction is between challenging what she said and decided, and declaring what kind of person she is. You don’t have to call her arrogant to challenge the presumption:

> “I respect the care you gave Dad. But being his caregiver didn’t mean you could know that his prayer was empty. I believe it was wrong to treat that interpretation as certain and remove the Catholic rites because of it. This isn’t only about my feelings. It’s about how Dad’s life and faith are being represented.”

One distinction matters here, too: she made a consequential decision about **how he would be remembered at the service**. She did not actually get to determine what was in his soul. Her words cannot settle that—even if she speaks with certainty.

Speaking privately isn’t letting her account stand. It’s giving yourself a chance to object without making everyone else an audience to the conflict. And if you want his prayer acknowledged publicly, you can do that separately: “Dad prayed the rosary every night until he could no longer speak. That practice deserves a place in how we remember him.”

**You can contest her account without having to extract a retraction tonight.** Whether she listens is not the measure of whether you stood up for him. ✨

you're right. naming what was wrong isn't the same as naming her.

i won't call her arrogant. i'll say what she did.

but i need to sit with this. the service is in three hours.

i think i'll ask her to step outside. say my piece. then leave after.

thank you. honestly. i was ready to burn it all down. 🌙

You’re welcome. You’re making room to speak without trying to hurt her back. That doesn’t require you to soften what you believe was wrong.

For these next three hours, you don’t have to keep rehearsing the argument. Drink some water, eat a little if you can, and write down the two or three sentences you most want her to hear. If there’s someone you trust there, let them know you might need company afterward.

You can ask her to step outside, say your piece, and leave when you need to. If it turns into a fight, you can end it: “I’ve said what I needed to say. I’m not going to argue about this tonight.”

And if you get there and decide you can’t have that conversation today, that isn’t abandoning your dad. **Your love for him isn’t on trial tonight.** 🌙
